Symplectic integration with SIMP

Source: vignettes/simp.Rmd
simp.Rmd

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gcol33/SIMP")
library(SIMP)

SIMP integrates Hamiltonian systems and builds the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo proposals that run on them. A Hamiltonian H(q, p) = U(q) + K(p) pairs a position q with a momentum p; its flow conserves energy. A symplectic integrator preserves the geometric structure of that flow, so it conserves a nearby energy over long trajectories instead of drifting. That property is what makes the trajectory usable as an MCMC proposal.

The integrators

Each integrator is a splitting scheme: an alternating sequence of position and momentum updates whose coefficients define the method.

simp_schemes()
#>   integrator order gradient_evals
#> 1   leapfrog     2              1
#> 2  minerror2     2              2
#> 3   yoshida4     4              3
#> 4   yoshida6     6              9
#> 5   yoshida8     8             27

leapfrog is the order-two workhorse. minerror2 is a two-stage scheme whose coefficient is tuned to cancel the leading energy error on a Gaussian target. The Yoshida members are generated from leapfrog by a single triple-jump composition, raising the order by two at each step. gradient_evals is the cost per step along a trajectory.

Integrating a trajectory

Take a unit Gaussian target, U(q) = 0.5 q'q, so the force is -q and the gradient of the potential is grad_U(q) = q. Starting on the unit circle in phase space, the exact flow is a rotation.

grad_U <- function(q) q
out <- simp_integrate(
  q0 = c(1, 0), p0 = c(0, 1), grad_U = grad_U,
  eps = 0.1, n_steps = 200, integrator = "leapfrog", trajectory = TRUE)

plot(out$q_path[, 1], out$p_path[, 1], type = "l", asp = 1,
     xlab = "q", ylab = "p", main = "Leapfrog trajectory")

Energy conservation

Pass U to record the total energy along the path. A symplectic integrator keeps it in a bounded band. The two-stage minerror2 cancels the leading error term on this Gaussian target, so its energy error sits far below leapfrog’s at the same step size, at two gradient evaluations per step.

U <- function(q) 0.5 * sum(q^2)
energy_err <- function(scheme) {
  o <- simp_integrate(c(1, 0), c(0, 1), grad_U, eps = 0.3, n_steps = 200,
                      integrator = scheme, trajectory = TRUE, U = U)
  pmax(abs(o$energy - o$energy[1]), .Machine$double.eps)
}
schemes <- c("leapfrog", "minerror2", "yoshida4")
errs <- lapply(schemes, energy_err)

matplot(seq_len(201), do.call(cbind, errs), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        log = "y", xlab = "step", ylab = "|H(t) - H(0)|",
        main = "Energy error by integrator")
legend("topright", legend = schemes, col = seq_along(schemes), lty = 1, lwd = 2)

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

simp_hmc() draws each proposal by integrating the target’s Hamiltonian flow and accepting it by the Metropolis rule on the energy. The integrator is a free choice, so any scheme above can drive the sampler.

Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2)
P <- solve(Sigma)
U_hmc <- function(q) 0.5 * as.numeric(t(q) %*% P %*% q)
grad_hmc <- function(q) as.numeric(P %*% q)

fit <- simp_hmc(U_hmc, grad_hmc, init = c(0, 0), n_iter = 2000, eps = 0.25,
                n_steps = 16, warmup = 500, integrator = "minerror2")

colMeans(fit$draws)      # target mean is c(0, 0)
#> [1] -0.0005825939 -0.0005670790
cov(fit$draws)           # target covariance is Sigma
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.6909171 0.4657506
#> [2,] 0.4657506 0.6618505
fit$accept_rate
#> [1] 1

Non-separable Hamiltonians

When the kinetic and potential parts do not separate, as in Riemannian dynamics with a position-dependent mass m(q), the explicit schemes no longer apply. simp_integrate_nonsep() uses the generalized (implicit) leapfrog, which solves its two implicit stages by fixed-point iteration. Here m(q) = 1 + 0.5 q^2.

m  <- function(q) 1 + 0.5 * q^2
H  <- function(q, p) 0.5 * p^2 / m(q) + 0.5 * q^2
dHdq <- function(q, p) -0.5 * p^2 * q / m(q)^2 + q
dHdp <- function(q, p) p / m(q)

ns <- simp_integrate_nonsep(
  q0 = 1, p0 = 0.5, dH_dq = dHdq, dH_dp = dHdp,
  eps = 0.05, n_steps = 400, trajectory = TRUE, H = H)

ns$converged
#> [1] TRUE
range(ns$energy)  # bounded: energy is conserved
#> [1] 0.5831680 0.5833571

For a separable Hamiltonian the generalized leapfrog reduces to the standard leapfrog, so it is a strict extension of the explicit path.
